subject: chem
title: Hydrocarbons
subtitle: Alkanes and alkenes: structure, reactions and mechanisms.
concept: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons; they undergo free radical substitution with halogens in UV light.
Alkenes contain a C=C double bond and undergo electrophilic addition; the π bond is the reactive site.
The mechanism of electrophilic addition explains regioselectivity (Markovnikov's rule) via carbocation stability.

notes.heading: Alkanes — Properties and Free Radical Substitution
items: Alkanes (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂) contain only σ bonds — all C–C and C–H single bonds. They are relatively unreactive due to the strong, non-polar bonds. Complete combustion produces CO₂ and H₂O; incomplete combustion produces CO and soot.

Free radical substitution (with Cl₂ or Br₂) requires UV light to initiate. Initiation: UV cleaves Cl₂ homolytically → 2Cl• (radicals). Propagation: Cl• + CH₄ → •CH₃ + HCl; then •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl• (chain reaction). Termination: two radicals combine → no new radicals formed. Products are a mixture of mono- and poly-substituted compounds.

notes.heading: Alkenes — Electrophilic Addition
items: Alkenes (CₙH₂ₙ) contain a C=C double bond (1 σ + 1 π). The π bond has high electron density above and below the plane — it is easily attacked by electrophiles.

Mechanism of electrophilic addition: the electrophile (e.g. Br₂, HBr) is attracted to the π electrons. The π bond breaks; both electrons go to form a bond with the electrophile → a carbocation intermediate forms. The counter-ion (nucleophile) then attacks the carbocation.

Markovnikov's rule: in addition of HX to an unsymmetrical alkene, H adds to the carbon with more H atoms (giving the more stable, more substituted carbocation). The major product is therefore the one derived from the more stable intermediate.
Carbocation stability: tertiary (3 alkyl groups) > secondary > primary — alkyl groups donate electron density by the inductive effect, stabilising the positive charge.

notes.heading: Tests and Other Reactions
items: Test for alkene: bromine water decolourises in the dark (orange → colourless). Alkanes do not react with bromine water in the dark (only in UV light — free radical substitution).
Hydrogenation: alkene + H₂ → alkane (Ni catalyst, ~150 °C). Used to harden vegetable oils.
Hydration: alkene + H₂O → alcohol (H₃PO₄ catalyst, high temperature and pressure). Polymerisation: many alkene molecules join via addition polymerisation across the C=C bond.

definitions.body: A species with an unpaired electron, denoted by a dot (e.g. Cl•); highly reactive.
A reaction in which an electrophile attacks the electron-rich π bond of an alkene, resulting in addition of atoms across the double bond.
In addition of HX to an unsymmetrical alkene, H adds to the carbon bearing more hydrogen atoms (giving the more stable carbocation intermediate).
A positively charged carbon species (carbenium ion); stability increases with the number of alkyl groups attached (tertiary > secondary > primary).

workedExamples.q: Write the mechanism for the reaction of propene (CH₃CH=CH₂) with HBr and explain the major product.

steps.text: HBr acts as electrophile; H⁺ attacks the π bond. Two possible carbocations: CH₃CH⁺CH₃ (secondary) or CH₃CHCH₂⁺ (primary).
Secondary carbocation (CH₃CH⁺CH₃) is more stable → forms preferentially.
Br⁻ attacks the secondary carbocation → major product: CH₃CHBrCH₃ (2-bromopropane).

mistakes: Drawing curly arrows starting from a bond or atom rather than from the electron pair (lone pair or bond electrons).
Confusing free radical substitution (alkanes + halogen, UV light) with electrophilic addition (alkenes + electrophile).
Applying Markovnikov's rule incorrectly — H goes to the carbon with MORE hydrogens.
tips: Bromine water test: alkene decolourises in the dark; alkane does not (alkane only reacts in UV light).
Curly arrows show electron pair movement — head points to where the electrons go.
Carbocation stability: tertiary (3 alkyl groups) > secondary > primary — alkyl groups stabilise positive charge by inductive effect.

flashcards.q: What conditions are needed for free radical substitution of alkanes?
flashcards.a: UV light (to initiate homolytic cleavage of the halogen molecule).

flashcards.q: What is the test for an alkene and what is the observation?
flashcards.a: Add bromine water (orange): alkene decolourises it (turns colourless). Alkanes do not decolourise in the dark.
In addition of HX to an unsymmetrical alkene, H adds to the carbon with more H atoms (giving the more stable carbocation).

flashcards.q: What is a carbocation and what affects its stability?
flashcards.a: A positively charged carbon; stability: tertiary > secondary > primary (more alkyl groups donate electron density, stabilising the charge).

flashcards.q: Name the three steps of free radical substitution.
flashcards.a: Initiation (UV breaks Cl₂ → 2Cl•), propagation (Cl• reacts with alkane, producing new radicals), termination (two radicals combine).

flashcards.q: What is formed when an alkene reacts with H₂O in the presence of H₃PO₄?

questions.q: Which reagent and condition are needed to brominate methane?
questions.exp: Free radical substitution requires Br₂ (or Cl₂) in gaseous/liquid form and UV light to initiate homolytic fission.

questions.q: What is the major product of HBr addition to propene?
questions.exp: Markovnikov: H adds to CH₂ (more H), Br to CH (fewer H) → secondary carbocation → 2-bromopropane.

questions.q: In free radical substitution, which step produces two radicals from a non-radical molecule?
questions.exp: Initiation: UV light causes homolytic fission of Cl₂ → 2Cl• (each atom takes one electron).

questions.q: Which correctly explains why alkenes are more reactive than alkanes?
opts: C=C π bond has high electron density and is easily attacked by electrophiles
They have more H atoms to substitute
questions.exp: The π bond above and below the molecular plane has high electron density — it is an attractive target for electrophiles.

questions.q: Hydrogenation of an alkene requires which conditions?
questions.exp: Catalytic hydrogenation: alkene + H₂ with Ni catalyst at ~150°C (or Pt at room temperature) → alkane.

recall: Describe the mechanism of free radical substitution with examples.
Explain why alkenes undergo addition rather than substitution.
Write the mechanism for electrophilic addition of HBr to an unsymmetrical alkene.
Explain Markovnikov's rule using carbocation stability.
